A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same automated preference fine-tuning study, renamed CheXalign in v2. The main text, figures, tables, equations and appendices support comparison, including matching material moved between sections.

before.justification: v1 reports original alignment experiments, report-generation and auxiliary-task results, and a reader study involving four radiologists.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments with two base models, alternative preference judges, length control and CheXbert evaluation. Appendix B.4 distinguishes borrowed external comparator scores from the work's own results.

M1.justification: The core procedure—sample four reports, rank against a reference, and select the highest and lowest scoring candidates—is retained. v2 makes BERTScore a reported alternative preference judge and introduces LC-GREEN for configuration selection. Section 5.1 explicitly distinguishes this selection change from regenerating training preferences with LC-GREEN.

E1.justification: The same seven datasets, report-generation task and six auxiliary tasks remain. CheXagent-2 adds report generation conditioned on clinical indications, creating a limited additional input scenario within the retained task (v2 Sections 4.1–4.2 and Appendix B.1).

E2.justification: LC-DPO replaces SimPO in the reported algorithm comparisons; DPO, IPO, KTO and ORPO remain. v2 adds CheXagent-2 SFT comparisons and a CheXbert comparison against GPT-4V, MAIRA-1/2, Med-PaLM M at three sizes, and LLaVA-Rad. These external scores are borrowed, not reported as rerun experiments.

E3.justification: v2 replaces GREEN-guided configuration selection with LC-GREEN selection, adds LC-GREEN and macro/micro CheXbert F1 evaluation, and drops F1RadGraph, BioMedMLScore and the radiologist preference protocol. Its additional CheXagent-2 experiments use a 3B model, approximately 148k training examples and batch size 64; the retained CheXagent setup uses 8B, 80k and batch size 32.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses across judges and configurations, GREEN versus LC-GREEN selection, and category-level CheXbert results (Figure 3 and Tables 2 and 11). It removes v1's GREEN error-subcategory analysis, annotated clinical examples and reader preference-reason analysis (Table 5, Figures 4/6 and Appendix A.4), substantially changing the diagnostic evidence.

E5.justification: v1's 95% confidence intervals for auxiliary tasks and reader-study standard errors disappear. v2 introduces 90% CheXbert confidence intervals from 1000 bootstrap samples and discusses significance at the 10% level. It also explicitly identifies single-run validation and judge-optimization results; the bootstrap count does not establish additional training runs.

E6.justification: Many result entries are replaced or added. CheXagent+DPO's MIMIC-CXR GREEN score changes from 0.354 to 0.325 under revised configuration selection, rather than establishing a same-setting regression. New CheXbert results include an average of 56.4 for GREEN-judged CheXagent-2+DPO versus 55.1 for its SFT baseline. Auxiliary-task scores also change, while v1's reader win rates and several metric/error breakdowns are removed.

T1.justification: v2 introduces the mathematical definition LC-GREEN = GREEN / max(relative verbosity, 1), adds the LC-DPO objective and removes the SimPO objective. The existing RLHF/DPO derivation moves to Appendix A without substantive revision. No new theorem or proof is supplied.

C1.justification: The abstract and contributions shift from GREEN gains and radiologist preferences to a broader pipeline evaluated across judges and models, a new length-controlled metric, and claimed state-of-the-art CheXbert performance. v2 newly emphasizes the effectiveness of inexpensive general-domain judges and removes the reader-validated clinical contribution. Alignment preservation is framed primarily in terms of average performance.

C2.justification: v1's interpretations of radiologist preferences and ORPO's clinical factuality are removed. v2 adds explanations involving judge-specific overoptimization and CheXagent-2's length increases closing a reference-length gap. Its limitations explicitly treat automatic metrics as silver standards, identify expert evaluation as outstanding, and qualify the CheXagent-2 study as preliminary.

D1.justification: Appendix B substantially expands v1's brief implementation appendix with split counts, indication requirements, selected hyperparameters, prompt handling, sampling temperatures, decoding choices, metric packages/versions and checkpoint information. It also documents the added model's batch size and H100 hardware option. These disclosures do not by themselves establish changes to previously undocumented CheXagent settings.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around AI feedback and automated judges, including Constitutional AI, AlpacaFarm, RLAIF versus RLHF, and judge-grading taxonomies. It explicitly contrasts its reference-based unimodal judging with prior multimodal alignment work by Sun et al. The medical-model context expands, while SimPO, RadGraph and BioMedLM-related references and discussion are removed.

P1.justification: Beyond the CheXalign title and terminology changes, the abstract, contributions and substantial explanatory passages are rewritten. Methodology becomes a separate section, results are reorganized around length exploitation and judge generalization, theory moves to Appendix A, and implementation/results appendices are extensively restructured.

P2.justification: The main text switches to two columns. The pipeline diagram is revised, a judge-comparison diagram is added, and the length scatter plot is redesigned. Results tables are reorganized by judge and model, with monochrome formatting replacing colored improvement cells; clinical and density figures disappear. New Table 8 also inconsistently places CheXagent-2 score and length statistics under its headings.

improvement.justification: v2 tests a concrete response to verbosity exploitation, broadens judge/model analyses and substantially improves reproducibility documentation. However, it removes v1's independent four-radiologist evaluation and clinical error analyses, while dropping uncertainty intervals for auxiliary tasks. The revised models are assessed through automatic proxies, and v2 Section 7 explicitly leaves expert validation outstanding. The added evidence therefore cannot establish whether the revised approach resolves the clinical concerns exposed by v1, leaving the net quality direction uncertain.
